children.value: This section explains why exact nearest-neighbor search fails in high dimensions, with the geometry and statistics behind it, and it is here as background. The next section only needs its conclusions, so a reader focused on the search methods can skim or skip it. The next section opens with a short recap of what carries forward.

All the structures of the previous section were developed with two or three dimensions in mind. Their inventors argued with drawings in the plane: rectangles that enclose points, spheres that touch rectangles, regions that can be skipped. When feature vectors with dozens or hundreds of dimensions arrived, the natural expectation was that these arguments would carry over, and that an index would prune the search in 100 dimensions much as it does in 2. This intuition turned out to be wrong. This section shows why, first for distances and then for the dot product, and draws a conclusion that shapes the rest of the chapter: in high dimensions, the exact nearest neighbor is not worth chasing.

children.value: Nine hundred dimensions are common for features extracted from media. In such a space, a point we would call “close” by any 2D standard lies outside a radius that covers the entire square in 2D. Distances simply grow with the dimension, and they grow for all pairs of points alike.

Growing distances alone would only change the scale. The real problem is that the distances of all points to a query grow at the same pace, so they become ever more similar. A simple measure for this is the

children.value: The loss of contrast has two consequences. The first concerns the index structures of the previous section; the second concerns the meaning of the nearest neighbor itself.
Consequence 1: trees can no longer prune

children.label: Consequence 1: trees can no longer prune

children.value: The optimal algorithm of the previous section must inspect every node whose region intersects the NN-sphere, the sphere around the query that passes through the nearest neighbor. If the nearest neighbor is far away, this sphere is large, and few regions can be skipped. To estimate the cost, we use a simple model: the data space is the unit cube, the dimensions are independent and uniformly distributed, and we use Euclidean distance. In this model, the probability that a point falls into a region equals the region’s volume.

children.value: . Beyond that point, the hierarchy only adds overhead: why build a tree if every leaf must be read anyway? In practice the index loses even earlier. A full scan reads the data sequentially, while a tree reads its leaves one by one; once a tree must visit a sizeable fraction of its leaves, the scan is faster. Weber, Schek, and Blott showed that for uniform data this happens beyond roughly ten dimensions (see the Further Reading section of the chapter summary).

The second consequence is more fundamental. If all points are almost equally far from the query, the nearest neighbor is only marginally nearer than the rest. Proximity stops expressing similarity: a point that is
percent farther away than the nearest neighbor is not meaningfully less similar.

Real data is kinder than this model. The analysis above assumes uniformly distributed, independent dimensions, and real feature vectors and embeddings are neither. They form clusters: images of sunsets lie closer to each other than to images of forests, and documents about cardiology lie closer to each other than to documents about tax law. Relative to the uniform background, in which everything appears equally far away, the members of a cluster stand out as outliers with clearly smaller distances. This is why vector search works at all in high dimensions, and why the approximate methods of the next section can exploit the structure of the data.

Within such a cluster, however, the loss of contrast remains. The nearest neighbor and the next few points lie at almost the same distance from the query. The exact nearest neighbor is not necessarily the best match in the sense the user cares about; it is one good match among several that are about equally close. Spending a full scan, or a visit to every leaf, to determine which of them is nearest buys a distinction that carries little meaning.

children.value: The discussion now runs parallel to the one for distances. Vectors that live alone in their orthants are hard to group, because no two of them agree in all signs, and the loss of contrast again weakens the meaning of similarity. Real data again saves the method. The embeddings of related documents form clusters, and their cosine values stand far above the narrow band around zero that random pairs occupy. A relevant document is an outlier in the distribution of scores. But among these outliers, the top few scores lie close together, and the document with the highest score is not necessarily the best semantic match. Any of the top-

children.html: kkk

children.value: results may be an equally good, or even better, answer.
Good matches instead of the best match

children.label: Good matches instead of the best match

children.value: High-dimensional space does not behave like the plane on which our intuition was trained. Distances grow, their contrast fades, and directions become meaningless; index structures that prune well in 2D end up visiting every leaf. At the same time, the loss of contrast questions the goal itself. When the nearest neighbor is only marginally nearer than its competitors, chasing the exact nearest neighbor is wasted effort. What matters is to find good matches: points that clearly stand out from the uniform background, even if they are not provably the nearest.

relax the requirement further. A fast retriever based on embeddings collects candidates, and a reranker reorders them with a more precise but more expensive model. The retriever does not need to deliver the exact top-

children.html: kkk

children.value: in the exact order, as long as the good hits are among its candidates; the reranker restores the precision. Exact nearest-neighbor search is therefore rarely needed. Giving up exactness on purpose, and searching approximately for good matches, buys back the speed that the curse of dimensionality took away. This is the subject of the next section.
